---
title: "Animation with requestAnimationFrame"
---

Every SVG you have drawn so far holds still. The shapes appear, and there they
stay until a click or a redraw changes them. Year one already had moving
pictures: a ball crossing the p5.js canvas, bouncing off the walls forever.
The browser can do the same thing without p5.js, and the whole trick is one
function.

## A circle that slides away {#sec-animation-slide}

1. Create a new app `animation-experiment` from our template inside
   `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Slide</h1>
   <svg id="stage" viewBox="0 0 400 120" width="400" height="120" role="img" aria-label="A sliding circle">
     <circle id="ball" cx="20" cy="60" r="20" fill="tomato" />
   </svg>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   const ball = document.querySelector<SVGCircleElement>('#ball');

   if (!ball) {
     throw new Error('The stage has no ball');
   }

   let x = 20;

   const tick = () => {
     x += 2;
     ball.setAttribute('cx', String(x));
     requestAnimationFrame(tick);
   };

   requestAnimationFrame(tick);
   ```

4. Run `npm start`.

The circle glides to the right. It reaches the edge of the stage and keeps
going, and because the SVG cuts off everything outside its box, you watch the
ball slip out of the picture. Nothing has stopped, though. `tick` is still
running 60 times a second, and `x` is somewhere past 4000 by the time you read
this sentence.

## The bounce {#sec-animation-bounce}

Year one's ball turned around at the wall by flipping the sign of its
direction, and that idea moves over unchanged. Give the direction its own
variable and name the two numbers that describe the stage. Then check the wall
before you write the attribute:

```ts
const WIDTH = 400;
const R = 20;

let x = 20;
let dx = 2;

const tick = () => {
  x += dx;
  if (x > WIDTH - R || x < R) {
    dx = -dx;
  }
  ball.setAttribute('cx', String(x));
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
};
```

The ball now runs between the two walls and never leaves. The condition
compares against `WIDTH - R` and `R` rather than `WIDTH` and 0, so the ball's
edge touches the wall instead of its center sinking into it.

## You ask for each frame yourself {#sec-animation-loop}

p5.js hid the loop from you. You wrote a function called `draw` and p5.js
called it about 60 times a second, and the machinery that did the calling was
never on your screen.

`requestAnimationFrame` turns that around. You hand it a function, and the
browser calls that function exactly once, right before it paints the next
frame. Once, and then it forgets you. Another frame means another request,
which is why the last line inside `tick` is another
`requestAnimationFrame(tick)`. Every frame books the next one. Delete that
line and the ball moves two pixels and stops, with no error and no warning,
because a single frame is a perfectly legal thing to ask for.

The values that survive between frames live in `let` variables outside the
function. `x` and `dx` work exactly like the count in a click counter: the
function forgets everything when it returns, the variables do not.

A `while (true)` loop would look simpler, and it would freeze the page. Your
code and the browser's painting take turns on one thread, so a loop that never
returns never lets the browser paint.

## Frames are not all the same length {#sec-animation-delta}

`x += 2` means two pixels per frame. On a 60 Hz screen that adds up to 120
pixels per second, on a 144 Hz gaming monitor to 288, and on a busy machine to
whatever the browser manages. Speed in pixels per frame is speed you cannot
predict.

The browser passes your function one number, a reading from its own clock.
Keep the previous reading in a variable and subtract, and you know how long
the last frame really took. Then you can name the speed in pixels per second
and let the arithmetic handle the frame rate:

```ts
const SPEED = 150;

let lastTime = 0;

const tick = (timestamp: number) => {
  if (lastTime === 0) {
    lastTime = timestamp;
  }
  const deltaSeconds = (timestamp - lastTime) / 1000;
  lastTime = timestamp;

  x += SPEED * dx * deltaSeconds;
  ball.setAttribute('cx', String(x));
  requestAnimationFrame(tick);
};
```

`deltaSeconds` is the length of the frame that just went by. With `dx` holding
1 or -1 it now carries only the direction, and `SPEED` carries the speed. The
very first frame has no frame before it, so the guard sets `lastTime` to the
current reading and that frame moves the ball by nothing.

## Stopping the animation {#sec-animation-stop}

The simplest way to stop the chain is a flag the loop checks before it books
the next frame:

```ts
let running = true;

const tick = () => {
  // ... move the ball ...
  if (running) {
    requestAnimationFrame(tick);
  }
};
```

Set `running` to `false` and the animation ends after the current frame,
because nothing asks for another one. Starting again means calling
`requestAnimationFrame(tick)` once, and once only: two chains running side by
side move the ball twice per frame.

The browser also lets you call off a frame you have already booked, with
`cancelAnimationFrame`. What that function needs to know is research question
2 below.

## Moving a shape without touching `cx` {#sec-animation-transform}

Writing `cx` works for a circle. A rectangle would need `x` and `y`, and a
`<g>` group has no position attributes at all. The `transform` attribute moves
any of them:

```ts
ball.setAttribute('transform', `translate(${x} 0)`);
```

`translate(x y)` shifts the element away from where its own attributes put it,
so the circle stays at `cx="20"` and the transform decides where it appears.
For a group that is the only way to move all its children at once.

`transform` can turn a shape as well, with `rotate`. A rotation always needs a
point to turn around, and choosing that point is research question 3.

## Code or CSS {#sec-animation-css}

Not every moving thing needs a loop. You already met `transition` in the
layout chapter: it animates a change that something else makes, such as a
`:hover` rule or a class your code adds. For motion that just runs by itself,
CSS has `@keyframes` and the `animation` property:

```css
.beacon {
  animation: pulse 1.2s infinite;
}

@keyframes pulse {
  0% {
    opacity: 1;
  }

  50% {
    opacity: 0.3;
  }

  100% {
    opacity: 1;
  }
}
```

The `@keyframes` rule describes what the animation looks like at points along
its way, and the `animation` line names the rule, the length of one round, and
the number of repeats. The browser fills in everything between the steps.

Use CSS when the motion simply plays, such as a pulse or a spinner. Use
`requestAnimationFrame` when the motion depends on state or input, because a
`@keyframes` rule cannot ask where the wall is or which key the player is
holding down.

::: {.research title="What the browser hands you, and what it takes back"}
The two exercises below need four answers this chapter does not give. Without
them you cannot stop an animation cleanly, restart it without a jump, write a
`@keyframes` rule of your own, or turn a clock hand around the middle of its
face.

1. `requestAnimationFrame` calls your function with one number. What does that
   number measure, and does it keep counting while you are not asking for
   frames?
2. `cancelAnimationFrame` takes one argument. What is it, and where in your
   code do you get hold of that value?
3. The SVG attribute `transform="rotate(...)"` accepts either one number or
   three. What do the second and third numbers stand for, and which point does
   the browser turn around when you write only the first?
4. A `@keyframes` rule lists the steps of an animation. What is the smallest
   number of steps a useful rule needs, and which two keywords can stand in
   for `0%` and `100%`?

The `rotate` question comes back in every exam task that turns something, so
that one has to work without looking it up.
:::

## Exercise: a bouncing ball {#sec-animation-ball}

Year one's diagonal ball, rebuilt in SVG and with a Start/Stop button.

1. Create a new app from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Bouncing ball</h1>

   <svg id="stage" viewBox="0 0 400 300" width="400" height="300" role="img" aria-label="A bouncing ball">
     <circle id="ball" cx="60" cy="60" r="20" fill="tomato" />
   </svg>

   <p>
     <button id="toggleButton" type="button">Start</button>
   </p>

   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Create `src/styles.css` and give `#stage` a white background and a solid
   border, so you can see the walls. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with
   `import './styles.css';`. Run `npm start`: one red ball sits in the corner
   of a bordered box.
4. Select the circle with `document.querySelector<SVGCircleElement>` and the
   button with `document.querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>`, and throw an error
   when either one is missing.
5. Add the constants `WIDTH`, `HEIGHT`, and `R`, one more for the speed in
   pixels per second, and the `let` variables `x`, `y`, `dx`, `dy`, and
   `lastTime`. Give `dx` and `dy` the value 1, so they carry only the
   direction.
6. Write `const tick = (timestamp: number) => { ... };` that computes
   `deltaSeconds` the way this chapter shows, moves `x` and `y`, and writes
   both `cx` and `cy` with `setAttribute`. End it with
   `requestAnimationFrame(tick)`.
7. Bounce off all four walls with two separate `if` statements: one for the
   side walls that flips `dx`, one for the top and bottom that flips `dy`.
   Merged into one condition, a touch of the side wall would flip the vertical
   direction too, and the ball would stagger along the edge.
8. Start the animation with one `requestAnimationFrame(tick)` at the end of
   the file. The ball travels diagonally and leaves every wall at the mirrored
   angle.
9. Now the button takes over, so delete that start call again. Keep the id of
   the booked frame in a `let` variable that begins at 0, and let 0 mean "not
   running", because the browser never hands out 0 as a frame id. The button's
   `click` listener starts the chain when the variable is 0 and calls
   `cancelAnimationFrame` otherwise, and it swaps the button's `textContent`
   between `Start` and `Stop`.
10. Test the restart. The ball jumps right across the box on the first frame
    after a pause, because the browser's clock kept running while your
    animation did not. Set `lastTime` back to 0 on every start.
11. While the ball moves it should breathe. In `src/styles.css`, write a
    `@keyframes` rule named `pulse` with two steps, from full opacity to about
    `0.4`, and a rule `#ball.moving` that plays it with
    `animation: pulse 0.8s infinite alternate;`. The click listener adds the
    class `moving` on start and removes it on stop.

### Optional: a speed slider {#sec-animation-ball-slider}

1. Add a slider under the button in `index.html`:

   ```html
   <p>
     <label for="speedRange">Speed</label>
     <input id="speedRange" type="range" min="20" max="600" step="10" value="150">
   </p>
   ```

2. Turn your speed constant into a `let` variable and give it the slider's
   `valueAsNumber` as its starting value.
3. Give the slider an `input` listener that writes `speedRange.valueAsNumber`
   into that variable. Drag the slider while the ball flies: the ball speeds
   up and slows down under your finger, and it never changes direction,
   because the sign lives in `dx` and `dy`.

## Exercise: a clock {#sec-animation-clock}

{{< exercise svg-clock >}}

The `index.html` you copied holds a 200 by 200 SVG with a face, 12 marks
around it, and three hands drawn as `<line>` elements with the ids `hourHand`,
`minuteHand`, and `secondHand`. All three point straight up at 12, and the
middle of the face sits at 100, 100 in the SVG's coordinate system.

1. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with `import './styles.css';` and run
   `npm start`. You see a clock face whose three hands all point at 12.
2. Select the three hands with `document.querySelector<SVGLineElement>` and
   throw an error when one of them is missing.
3. Write `const update = () => { ... };`. Inside it, read the current time
   with `const now = new Date();` and pull the three numbers you need out of
   it with `now.getHours()`, `now.getMinutes()`, and `now.getSeconds()`.
4. Turn each number into an angle in degrees, measured clockwise from 12:

   * the second hand: `seconds * 6`, because a full turn is 360 degrees and a
     minute has 60 seconds;
   * the minute hand: `minutes * 6 + seconds * 0.1`, so the hand creeps
     forward during the minute instead of jumping;
   * the hour hand: `(hours % 12) * 30 + minutes * 0.5`. The `% 12` folds
     afternoon hours back onto the face, and the minutes carry the hand from
     one hour mark towards the next.
5. Give each hand a `transform` attribute that rotates it by its angle around
   the middle of the face. Question 3 of the research task tells you how to
   name that point. Reload the page: the clock shows the current time.
6. Call `update` from a `requestAnimationFrame` loop, the same shape as the
   ball's `tick`. The second hand still jumps once per second, even though
   your code now recomputes the angles 60 times a second. Three `setAttribute`
   calls per frame with values the browser already has cost almost nothing,
   and the next step pays them back.

### Optional: a smooth second hand {#sec-animation-clock-smooth}

`now.getMilliseconds()` gives you the part of the second that has passed. Add
it to your seconds value as a fraction of a second before you compute the
angle, and the second hand sweeps instead of ticking. That sweep is what the
loop bought you, because one update per second leaves nothing to glide
between.
